data.title: Ford battery study: Mustang Mach-E batteries retain 92 per cent capacity after five years
data.description:
Ford says its earliest Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs have retained an average 92 per cent of their usable battery capacity after more than five years, based on an analysis of approximately 36,000 vehicles in the United States and Canada.

The findings provide a substantial body of real-world evidence on EV battery ageing, with the 2021-model vehicles collectively covering about 3.2 billion kilometres.

Ford’s analysis found 95 per cent of the vehicles had battery health between 87 and 97 per cent, indicating most retained a large proportion of their original usable capacity.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: Ford’s Super Mustang Mach-E the only EV running at Pikes Peak Hill Climb. Guess who won?
READ MORE: Jeepers Ford! The frunk is now a $700 option for the 2026 Mustang Mach-E!
READ MORE: 2026 Ford Mustang Mach-E Review: Updated electric SUV aims to stand out from the Tesla crowd

The results also extended to vehicles with unusually high mileages.

More than 2000 owners had travelled beyond 161,000km on their original battery, with those vehicles retaining an average of more than 91 per cent battery health.

A much smaller group of more than 30 drivers had passed 322,000km, averaging 88 per cent.

The figures come from Ford’s own analysis, rather than an independent study, and relate to North American vehicles. The data was collected as of August 2026, with an average ownership period of 5.2 years.

Battery state of health in this case refers to remaining usable capacity. It is not a direct measurement of driving range, which also depends on conditions and vehicle efficiency.

Nor do the findings establish how many batteries have needed replacement: Ford identifies the high-mileage groups as using their original batteries, but does not publish a battery replacement rate for the entire cohort.

Ford’s technical leader of high-voltage battery cells and systems, Kevin Vander Laan, said looking beyond the average was important.

“Averages can hide variation, so that range matters,” he said.

The analysis followed the experience of Mustang Mach-E owner David Blenkle, whose 2022-model vehicle has covered more than 644,000km on its original battery.

Ford says Blenkle’s battery health remains strong, although it does not provide a specific percentage. His vehicle is also separate from the 2021-model group examined in the larger study.

Across its broader battery-electric vehicle line-up released in the US and Canada over the past five years, Ford says batteries are retaining an average of more than 90 per cent health at approximately 161,000km.

The company says its packs are designed to last at least 10 years. That is a design target, rather than a lifespan demonstrated by this five-year data set.

For Australian buyers, Ford lists an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty, whichever comes first.

The 2021 Mach-E vehicles in the analysis use nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) battery chemistry. Their results should not automatically be applied to newer vehicles with different battery types.

Ford recommends AC home charging for everyday use, reserving DC fast charging for when it is needed, and preconditioning the vehicle while plugged in to help manage temperature extremes.

It also advises owners to follow the charging recommendations for their particular vehicle. Frequent full charges are generally unnecessary for the NCM batteries in the study, while some newer Ford EVs use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries that benefit from occasional charging to 100 per cent to help calibrate the battery management system.

data.title: Wey wait: GWM’s luxury push slips to 2027 as 550kW flagship SUV enters the frame
data.description:
GWM’s premium Wey brand will not hit its stride in Australia until 2027, with its model line-up, launch timing and dealer arrangements still being finalised.

The G9 hybrid and plug-in hybrid people-mover remains on track for a low-key introduction, with pricing expected before the end of 2026. But the broader product rollout and promotional push will follow next year.

A potential headline act is the V9X, a six-seat plug-in hybrid luxury SUV packing up to 550kW and 930Nm.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: It’s another giant Chinese PHEV SUV! And the GWM Wey V9X is a real chance to come to Australia
READ MORE: Wey the latest Chinese brand to announce Aussie launch: GWM goes upmarket
READ MORE: GWM’s EV and PHEV push: Ora Touring and bigger Jolion spearhead 16-product Australian expansion

GWM Australia marketing and communications chief Steve Maciver said establishing Wey required more than simply introducing its first vehicle.

“In terms of launching a new sub-brand, that doesn’t happen overnight, so we’ve just got to make sure we get that right.”

Originally announced in October 2025 for a 2026 Australian arrival, Wey will compete with premium Chinese brands including BYD’s Denza and other 2027 newcomers including Avatr and Exlantix.

Maciver confirmed the V9X was under consideration as GWM builds a broader luxury range.

“It’s an incredible product. It’s an incredible, large SUV. We’re considering that,” he said.

“That’s on the radar. When we see a product like that, which can be made available to us, if we’ve got an ambition to be a top three brand, we’d be crazy not to have a look at that.”

Offered in China in 5205mm and 5299mm lengths, the V9X combines a 2.0-litre turbo-petrol engine with two electric motors and all-wheel drive.

Depending on the version, claimed electric range stretches from 240km to 363km on the WLTC test cycle. The flagship claims 0-100km/h in 4.6 seconds and a 30-80 per cent recharge in nine minutes.

Chinese-market equipment includes air suspension, adaptive dampers, rear-wheel steering, massaging seats, second-row captain’s chairs, a refrigerator and a 31-speaker sound system. Australian specifications remain unconfirmed.

Wey vehicles will be sold through selected existing GWM dealers, joining a portfolio that already includes Haval, Tank, Ora and Cannon.That’s unlike arch-rival Chery which is retaiing its myriad brands though multiple dealer networks.

“We will insist on one GWM. Our strategy is different from others,” said GWM Australia managing director Andrew Gao.

Wey models form part of GWM’s planned 14 new or updated Australian models in 2027, as it targets a climb from seventh to fifth in the sales rankings.

But Maciver said the priority was securing a sustained product rollout.

“We’ve got to understand what’s Wey’s future 12, 18, 24 months ahead and that’s the bit we’re trying to work through now, just to give us certainty that we’re ready.”

data.title: Musk expands Tesla autonomy plan: Announces Model Y without a steering wheel as US$29,990 Cybercab goes on sale
data.description:
Tesla is planning a driverless version of its best-selling Model Y SUV with room for six or seven people, as it starts taking orders from selected US customers for the two-seat Cybercab at US$29,990 ($45,000 approx) plus a mandatory US$299 ($450) monthly fee.

Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit on November 18, Tesla chief executive Elon Musk said the larger vehicle would cater for families and groups who couldn’t fit in a Cybercab.

“So what we plan to do is have an autonomous version of Model Y that wouldn’t have steering wheels and pedals, and would be good for transporting groups of six or seven people,” Musk said.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: 2026 Tesla Model Y L Review: Six-seater version of Australia’s top-selling EV adds to the appeal
READ MORE: Tesla Cybercab in Australia: Our man Corby meets the future and comes away disturbed
READ MORE: Elon Musk excited about being asleep at the wheel as he launches Tesla Cybercab

Musk gave no launch date or price and did not say whether Tesla would sell the driverless Model Y to private buyers. He separately suggested Tesla could shift all Model Y production to the longer Model Y L, which is already sold in Australia as a six-seater.

Tesla announced the Cybercab offer through its Robotaxi account on X on November 13, inviting selected US customers to buy the two-seat EV for personal use. Its order page listed December deliveries in Austin, Texas, and required a US$1000 ($1500) non-refundable deposit. The first month of the subscription is included.

The Cybercab has no steering wheel or pedals. Owners use the Tesla app to set a destination, and the car can travel only within areas Tesla enables. At the advertised rate, the required subscription adds US$3588 ($5400) a year to the cost of using the car.

“Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription,” Tesla’s agreement says. The subscription enables autonomous driving and connectivity.

The sales offer comes as the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration examines Tesla’s certification that the Cybercab meets federal vehicle safety standards. One of the regulator’s questions is how the car complies with a braking standard that specifies a foot control. Tesla submitted its response on October 30 and requested confidential treatment.

Separately, US electric vehicle website Electrek identified eight Cybercab crash reports in the regulator’s public data. Four involved the automated driving system in Austin, with no injuries reported. In two of those cases, another vehicle hit a stationary Cybercab.

The other four involved test vehicles with a human driver and Level 2 driver assistance engaged. Two reports recorded minor injuries. Another listed a Cybercab travelling at 53mph (85km/h) in a collision on a Philadelphia highway, with injuries listed as unknown. The public reports leave the cause of those crashes undetermined.

Tesla put the Cybercab on display in Melbourne this month. The purchase invitation is limited to selected US customers, and Tesla has announced no Australian price or launch date.

data.title: BYD Ti7 latest: Banned from sale in Europe, confirmed for 2027 sale in Australia!
data.description:
The BYD Ti7 plug-in SUV that has just been banned from sale in the EU has been confirmed to go on sale in Australia in the first quarter of 2027.

Speaking to EV Central before a Dutch court ordered a halt to sales of the Ti7 in the European Union over its resemblance to the Land Rover Defender, BYD Australia chief operating officer Stephen Collins said the green light for the seven-seat SUV had been given.

“We’re hoping to have it in the market certainly in the first quarter,” Collins said. “Not early, but probably more late in the first quarter.”

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: JLR v BYD update: JLR ordered to destroy seized BYD files as Ti7 Defender dispute continues
READ MORE: Legal action! BYD Ti 7 PHEV wagon homologated for Australia as JLR pursues Defender claim
READ MORE: BYD’s Fang Cheng Bao Titanium 7 launched: All-electric Toyota Prado rival shapes up for Aussie arrival as a Denza

Collins said the Ti7 would give BYD a more traditionally styled seven-seat SUV alongside the Sealion 8.

“It’ll be towards the top of our range. It’s, you know, for want of a better term, a boxier style, larger SUV, seven-seater,” he said.

“We’ll make it really good value for money. It’ll sit really well alongside Sealion 8.”

Collins said BYD had yet to finalise Australian pricing. Asked whether the Ti7 would cost more than the Sealion 8 or be priced close to it, he said: “Not sure yet.”

“It’s been very successful in a lot of other markets. So we think it’ll fit really nicely into the range.”

The Ti range originates with BYD’s Fang Cheng Bao brand in China, where the Ti7 went on sale in 2025. The newest and largest model is the Ti9, a 5.27-metre six-seat plug-in hybrid SUV launched in China on November 19.

Collins said the Ti9 was “not currently on the agenda” for Australia. Asked about the forthcoming Ti6 and smaller Ti3 SUVs as well, he said:

“Not in the foreseeable future.

“We’re not looking at this point at any other Tis,” he said.

Two Fang Cheng Bao models are already sold in Australia. The Bao 5 and Bao 8 off-road SUVs are badged here as the Denza B5 and B8.

Collins was speaking about the Ti7 after the controversy over its design had first blown up in Europe, but before the November 20 preliminary ruling in which the District Court of The Hague found the Ti7 infringed Jaguar Land Rover’s registered EU design for the current-generation Defender.

The judge found that the Ti7 shared distinctive elements of the Defender’s design and that the differences identified by BYD did too little to change the overall impression.

The injunction takes effect one week after the judgment is formally served and also bars BYD from building the Ti7 at its new plant in Hungary. JLR has six months to begin a full proceeding on the design claim. BYD maintains it designed the Ti7 independently and says it will appeal.

The Dutch order leaves BYD free to proceed with its UK launch, with customer deliveries planned from January 2027. The court found it had no jurisdiction over BYD’s UK subsidiary and rejected JLR’s claims against the Dutch BYD companies relating to the UK because there was insufficient evidence they were involved in offering the Ti7 there.

The injunction follows a separate ruling earlier in November that ordered JLR to arrange the destruction of digital files seized from two BYD offices in the Netherlands.

JLR brought the case in The Hague because BYD’s European and Dutch subsidiaries are based in the Netherlands. The court can issue EU-wide injunctions in disputes over registered EU designs.

As EV Central previously reported, Australian type approval covers front- and all-wheel drive versions of the Ti7, both with seven seats and a 110kW 1.5-litre turbo-petrol engine. The filing lists maximum outputs of 200kW and 300kW respectively. Australian battery capacity, electric driving range and charging specifications are yet to be announced.

data.title: Around the world with just 4.25 per cent battery degradation: Volkswagen ID.Buzz clocks almost 100,000km across 92 countries
data.description:
A Volkswagen ID.Buzz has completed an almost 100,000km journey through 92 countries with no technical breakdowns and its battery still recording 95.75 per cent state of health, according to Volkswagen.

German long-distance driver Rainer Zietlow’s electric world tour covered 99,767km across six continents, including Australia, earning a Guinness World Record for the most countries visited in a continuous journey by a battery-powered electric vehicle.

But for potential EV buyers concerned about battery longevity, the inspection after the journey arguably provides the more interesting number.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: Electric Kombi camper revealed: Volkswagen ID. California Cruise sleeps two, powers a campsite and runs its climate control for 48 hours
READ MORE: Volkswagen ID.Buzz Good-Night Pack: This is the official camper conversion the all-electric Kombi always deserved
READ MORE: 2025 Volkswagen ID.Buzz Pro Review: Head-turning love for the born-again Kombi

Volkswagen says German inspection organisation TÜV Nord assessed the high-voltage battery’s state of health at 95.75 per cent after the trip.

That equates to a reported 4.25 per cent reduction from full battery health after close to 100,000km of driving through conditions ranging from deserts to mountain regions.

It is a result from one vehicle rather than a fleet-wide battery study, and Volkswagen’s release does not detail the assessment method or provide a measured starting state of health.

Nevertheless, it offers an encouraging example of an EV battery coping with intensive use across varied climates.

The record vehicle was a long-wheelbase ID.Buzz Pro, which Volkswagen describes as being in standard production condition.

The journey involved more than 300 charging cycles and 16 container-ship crossings, so the around-the-world description includes substantial sea transport between driving legs.

Volkswagen says the vehicle completed the trip without a single technical breakdown.

Zietlow, who has undertaken projects exclusively with Volkswagen vehicles since 2005, said reliability was the standout feature.

Charging access proved considerably less consistent.

In countries including Zambia and Tanzania, Zietlow said the lack of public charging infrastructure meant arranging supervised charging at electricity substations.

That is an important qualification for anyone interpreting the record as evidence that an international electric road trip now requires little planning.

The journey demonstrates what is possible with preparation and support, while also highlighting how much charging availability still varies between countries.

Zietlow reported more developed charging networks in South Africa, Morocco and Rwanda, and substantial progress in Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Chile.

The Australian leg also features in Volkswagen’s photographic record of the trip.

For local buyers, the useful takeaway is the combination of distance covered, reported reliability and the battery assessment afterwards.

data.title: World debut: Honda returns to Australia’s large SUV market with new-generation-hybrid Avancier
data.description:
Honda has unveiled the all-new Avancier, a three-row hybrid SUV that will introduce the company’s next-generation petrol-electric system and return it to Australia’s large SUV market in April 2027.

The Avancier will sit above the CR-V, ZR-V and HR-V as Honda’s fourth SUV line in Australia. It will be the brand’s first large SUV here since the V6-powered MDX was discontinued in 2007.

EV Central covers plugless hybrids selectively, but the Avancier warrants a closer look. It introduces a new design and gives electric drive a bigger role in Honda’s hybrid system. It also returns Honda to an important segment at a time when its Australian sales recovery has slowed.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: Honda plans hybrid expansion to tackle Toyota, bringing EVs to challenge Tesla
READ MORE: Honda CR-V and ZR-V two-pronged electrified attack on Toyota RAV4 hybrid
READ MORE: We want our people back! Honda Australia boss says going EV in 2026 will return fans to the brand

The biggest change to the hybrid system is at the rear axle. The Avancier uses a dedicated electric motor to drive the rear wheels, rather than the propeller shaft used to transmit drive to the rear axle in the current CR-V e:HEV AWD.

Honda says the new arrangement allows it to vary the torque delivered to each axle more quickly and precisely. The company also says the revised petrol engine operates efficiently across a wider range of speeds and loads, while the hybrid drive unit is smaller and more efficient.

Honda is targeting a fuel economy improvement of more than 10 per cent for a next-generation hybrid model combining the new system, platform and electric all-wheel drive. It has yet to release an Australian fuel consumption figure for the Avancier.

The Avancier is the first of 15 models Honda plans to launch globally with its new hybrid technology by the end of March 2030. At the same time, Honda has scaled back its EV rollout, including cancelling most models in the futuristic 0 Series.

It sells no PHEVs in Australia and one EV, the tiny and supply-limited Super-One.

In Australia, the new SUV gives Honda an entry in a segment that includes the Toyota Kluger, Hyundai Santa Fe and Kia Sorento hybrids, as well as the BYD Sealion 8 plug-in hybrid.

Honda delivered 12,919 vehicles in Australia through October, up just 34 vehicles, or 0.3 per cent, on the same period last year. October deliveries fell 11.2 per cent to 1135.

Annual sales had risen from a low of 13,734 in 2023 to 15,383 in 2025. That remains well below the 43,868 vehicles Honda delivered in 2019, before its July 2021 switch from franchised dealers to fixed-price agency sales.

“As we continue to expand our product lineup, we are excited to add a large SUV to our offering for consumers. Our commitment to hybrid is stronger than ever and you can see that come to fruition with the all-new Honda Avancier,” said Honda Australia director of automotive Robert Thorp.

The Avancier introduces a new design direction for Honda, including a redesigned badge. It is a separate model from the Avancier coupe-style SUV sold by Honda’s joint venture with GAC in China.

Honda has confirmed a head-up display, a 15-inch infotainment screen and what it calls relaxation seats. Australian pricing, dimensions, power outputs and the full equipment list are still to come.

The vehicle on display was badged RS, which is usually reserved for flagship models in a range.

data.title: Smaller motors, cheaper EVs? ZF’s 30,000rpm electric drive targets mainstream cars
data.description:
A new electric drive from German automotive supplier ZF is claimed to make EV motors smaller, lighter and cheaper without sacrificing power, potentially giving car-makers more room to work with and less expensive hardware to install.

Called the High Revolution Drive, the system spins its motor at up to 30,000rpm and is aimed at high-volume passenger cars with outputs of around 150-200kW, rather than being reserved for exotic performance models.

ZF claims the complete drive is almost 25 per cent smaller and lighter than a comparable unit from its existing SELECT family, while requiring half the magnet mass. Its product page also claims approximately 13 per cent lower system costs.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

Those are potentially meaningful savings for manufacturers trying to make electric cars more affordable, although a cheaper drive unit does not translate into an equivalent percentage reduction in the showroom price.

ZF is talking to several car-makers and targeting production by 2030.

The significance lies less in chasing a headline motor speed than in combining that speed with lower material use, compact packaging and efficiency comparable to the larger drive it could replace.

High-revving electric motors are already part of the industry’s development push. Xiaomi, for example, quotes speeds of up to 27,200rpm for its HyperEngine technology, showing ZF is advancing an established engineering approach rather than inventing a new way to propel an EV.

What makes ZF’s proposal noteworthy is its focus on the mainstream market and the claimed savings across the integrated drive system, which combines the motor, inverter and transmission.

The principle behind the smaller motor is straightforward. Power depends on both torque and rotational speed, so spinning faster allows a motor to produce the same power with less torque.

That enables a smaller motor, while reduction gearing converts its high-speed rotation into the torque needed to turn the wheels.

ZF uses two stages of reduction gearing with an overall ratio of about 18:1. The version it has shown produces a peak 200kW and 3500Nm at the wheels.

That wheel-torque figure is measured after the gearing multiplies the motor’s torque, so it should not be compared directly with the motor-torque figures normally quoted in EV specifications.

Similarly, the two-stage transmission refers to successive stages of reduction gearing; it does not establish that the vehicle has a two-speed gearbox that changes gear while driving.

ZF’s comparison is with a SELECT drive whose motor reaches 18,000rpm. The new unit’s 30,000rpm ceiling represents an increase of about 67 per cent.

Making that work presents challenges in controlling noise and vibration, which ZF says it has addressed by developing the motor, gearing, bearings and gear-tooth geometry together.

The company’s transmission experience is relevant here: making a motor spin faster is only useful if the complete drive remains quiet, durable and efficient enough for everyday cars.

ZF says the system achieves nearly 93 per cent efficiency, comparable with the existing SELECT drive.

That qualification matters when assessing the range potential. ZF is claiming a smaller and lighter drive with similar efficiency, rather than a large reduction in the electricity needed to deliver the same mechanical output.

Reducing weight could help driving range, and the smaller package could give vehicle designers more flexibility. However, ZF has not quantified an extra distance per charge or specified the weight saving in kilograms.

Nor does a drive unit that is 25 per cent lighter make the entire car 25 per cent lighter: the battery, body and other components still account for much of an EV’s mass.

The reduction in magnet requirements could be particularly useful commercially, cutting material costs and exposure to critical supply chains. ZF also identifies lower copper and iron consumption on its product page.

The High Revolution Drive is being developed as a variant of the modular SELECT platform, using existing technologies to limit development work and allow manufacturers to tailor it to different vehicles.

Its architecture can accommodate both 400-volt and 800-volt electrical systems, broadening the range of potential applications beyond cars using the latest high-voltage platforms.

data.title: Mercedes-AMG GT SUV Deep Dive: Why heat matters more than horsepower in this electric monster
data.description:
The Mercedes-AMG GT SUV can produce a staggering 860kW. But the more interesting question is what happens after the first few seconds of full-throttle acceleration.

Delivering enormous power in an electric vehicle is one challenge. Delivering it repeatedly, without the motors, battery and electronics overheating and forcing a reduction in output, is quite another.

That’s the engineering problem AMG is tackling with its new electric performance flagship. Alongside its 860kW peak output, the GT 63 SUV is rated at 530kW continuously, with an arsenal of compact axial-flux motors, individually cooled battery cells and sophisticated thermal management designed to keep the performance coming.

READ MORE: Best luxury EVs in Australia 2026: Premium electric cars under $100k, $150k, $250k and beyond, priced and compared

READ MORE: Unveiled: The new Mercedes-AMG GT 4-Door EV has so much tech it makes the Porsche Taycan look very yesterday
READ MORE: Is this the sensible supercar? Mercedes-AMG GT 53 EV revealed with less power but 112km more range than crazy axial-flux 860kW flagship
READ MORE: 2026 Porsche Cayenne Turbo EV Brief Drive: This vehicle is brilliant, but all sorts of wrong

The technology is significant beyond the headline numbers, although how effectively it works remains to be established in independent testing.

Mercedes-Benz Australia lists the GT SUV as coming soon, with local pricing and specifications still to be confirmed.

The GT SUV range comprises three all-wheel drive models. The entry-level GT 53 produces 400kW and 800Nm from two conventional electric motors, while the GT 55 steps up to three axial-flux motors producing 600kW and 1860Nm.

The flagship GT 63 uses the same three-motor configuration but increases peak output to 860kW and 2000Nm.

The GT 55 and GT 63 share a claimed continuous output of 530kW, despite their substantially different peak ratings.

All three models use 800-volt electrical architecture, with battery capacities of 106kWh or 128kWh depending on the variant.

Where the heat comes from

An EV converts stored electrical energy into motion through its battery, inverters and motors. Each stage incurs losses, some of which become heat that must be removed.

A short acceleration run can use some of the system’s capacity to absorb heat. Repeated acceleration or sustained high speed requires heat to be carried away quickly enough to prevent temperatures continually rising.

Cooling from inside the battery outwards

The battery’s ability to deliver power depends partly on the temperature of individual cells. An acceptable average pack temperature can conceal a local hot spot that forces the control system to reduce output.

Many liquid-cooled EV batteries transfer heat through a plate or other cooling structure adjoining the cells. AMG instead circulates electrically non-conductive oil directly around each cylindrical cell.

Both approaches must conduct heat out of the cell’s interior. Direct cooling brings the fluid to the cell casing, reducing the intervening structures through which that heat must pass.

AMG also uses narrow cells, measuring 26mm across and 105mm tall. Their diameter limits the distance between the core and the cooled outer surface. An aluminium casing helps conduct heat, while a full-tab design reduces internal electrical resistance, according to the company.

Moving heat is only the first step

Oil passing around the cells carries heat away from them, but the vehicle still has to dispose of that heat. Cooling capacity is also needed by the motors and their power electronics.

AMG’s Central Coolant Hub coordinates pumps, valves and sensors to allocate cooling according to demand. Its wider thermal system includes a chiller and main and auxiliary radiators.

If the battery is already at the required temperature, the system can direct cooling capacity towards the drive units. When several components are working hard, it must balance their competing needs.

Why the motors are shaped differently

The GT 55 and GT 63 use axial-flux motors developed from technology supplied by Mercedes-owned British specialist YASA.

Their disc-shaped layout places a stator between two magnet-equipped rotors, with magnetic flux running parallel to the shaft. The arrangement offers high torque and power density in a short package.

YASA identifies short copper windings and direct oil cooling as advantages for sustained output, helping remove heat before temperature becomes a constraint.

The rear drive unit combines two motors and their gearboxes, with oil cooling for the motors and gears. Water-cooled silicon-carbide inverters convert the battery’s direct current into the supply the motors require.

Separate rear motors allow driving force to be varied at each rear wheel, changing the turning effect on the vehicle and helping control its path.

Saving capacity for the useful parts of a lap

AMG’s Predictive Performance Manager adjusts power according to the track section, conserving electrical and thermal capacity where extra output offers little lap-time benefit.

A tight downhill sequence, for example, offers less opportunity to exploit full power than an uphill straight. Reducing demand in the former can leave more capacity available for the latter.

Controlling the body without conventional anti-roll bars

The GT 63’s Active Ride Control+ suspension uses a central pump, controlled valves and hydraulically interconnected dampers to generate forces opposing body movement. It replaces conventional anti-roll bars and is optional on the GT 55.

A mechanical anti-roll bar links suspension movement across an axle. It resists roll, but can also transmit a disturbance from one side towards the other. Hydraulic control allows AMG to vary the support according to the driving situation, including pitch under acceleration and braking.

Adjustable air springs control ride characteristics and height. The aim is support during manoeuvres with compliance over uneven roads.

The system still has to manage the SUV’s mass. Its effectiveness requires assessment of grip, ride quality and consistency, alongside how flat the body remains.

There is no confirmed timetable for this combination of motors, battery cooling and active suspension to reach affordable EVs. The demonstrated expansion is within AMG itself, from the electric GT 4-Door Coupe to the GT SUV.

data.title: Latest ANCAP results: BYD Sealion 8 puts BYD back on five-star footing after Sealion 5 setback
data.description:
BYD has bounced back from a three-star ANCAP setback with a five-star rating for the new Sealion 8.

ANCAP marked down the seven-seat plug-in hybrid SUV after the driver’s footwell split in a frontal crash test, but it retained the maximum rating.

But back in September the the smaller BYD Sealion 5 SUV, managed only three stars. Both SUVs were assessed under ANCAP’s latest 2026-2028 protocols.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: Three-star setback: BYD Sealion 5 breaks brand’s perfect ANCAP run as M9 people-mover scores five
READ MORE: GAC Aion UT and XPeng X9 earn five ANCAP stars under tougher 2026 safety tests, but where are the knobs?
READ MORE: Cheap EVs clear tougher new ANCAP safety tests: Geely EX2 and Leapmotor B05 score five stars

The split opened behind the brake and accelerator pedals. ANCAP said it did not increase the injury risk measured by the driver dummy, but warned such a failure can raise the risk of lower-leg injuries.

The Sealion 8 scored 90 per cent for crash protection, 76 per cent for crash avoidance, 73 per cent for safe driving and 100 per cent for post-crash safety. The rating covers all Australian and New Zealand variants.

The Sealion 5 remains the only model assessed under the new protocols to fall short of five stars, according to ANCAP. Its weakest scores were 48 per cent for safe driving and 51 per cent for crash avoidance.

The Sealion 8 also earned full marks for the layout and operation of its essential controls. That was an area where the five-star GAC Aion UT and XPeng X9 lost points in October over their reliance on touchscreens.

The electric GWM Ora 5 also earned five stars, covering both Lux and Ultra variants. It scored 91 per cent for crash protection and 92 per cent for post-crash safety.

ANCAP said its automatic emergency braking and lane-keeping systems generally performed well, although avoiding cars, motorcycles and pedestrians at lower speeds proved more challenging.

The Sealion 8 was tested by ANCAP, while the Ora 5 was tested by EuroNCAP and the results verified by the local safety authority.

data.title: Jetour TX electric SUV launches: Chery-owned SUV brand is coming to Australia and this is its first EV
data.description:
Jetour has opened Chinese pre-sales for its new TX electric SUV, adding a potential battery-powered contender to its Australian expansion plans as the Chery-owned brand prepares for its local debut.

Combining boxy styling, rear- and all-wheel drive options and a claimed driving range of up to 550km, the TX brings a dedicated electric platform to a brand whose initial Australian range is expected to centre on the T1 and T2 PHEV SUVs.

With the local launch only days away, Jetour Australia says there is no announcement on a local introduction for the TX.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: New 575kW Jetour Traveller 7 revealed: Rugged PHEV packs 245km EV range as Chinese brand prepares for Australia

“The TX shows the depth of Jetour’s global line-up, including its first fully electric SUV,” a Jetour Australia spokesperson told EV Central.

“We’re always looking at which models best suit Australian drivers, but we have nothing to announce on the TX at this stage.

“Jetour is coming to Australia with a line-up of adventure-ready SUVs built for the way Australians travel and explore, and we’ll share more about our Australian models very soon.”

Chinese pre-sales opened on November 16, with five variants priced from 99,900 to 145,900 yuan ($22.400 to $37,400 approx). Those are domestic pre-sale prices and provide no indication of what an Australian version might cost.

The TX’s upright body, circular lighting and contrasting exterior trim continue Jetour’s preference for rugged-looking SUVs, although this model is built on a purpose-designed rear-wheel drive electric platform.

It measures 1880mm wide and 1700mm tall, with a 2735mm wheelbase. Overall length is quoted at 4605mm including its tailgate-mounted storage box, or 4475mm without it – putting the body close to the size of a BYD Atto 3.

Rear-wheel drive versions produce 200kW and 285Nm, with a claimed 0-100km/h time of 7.5 seconds. The dual-motor all-wheel drive flagship lifts combined outputs to 275kW and 427Nm and cuts that sprint to 5.5 seconds.

The Chinese range comprises four rear-drive variants claiming 550km of range and an all-wheel drive version rated at 510km. Both figures use China’s relatively generous CLTC test cycle.

Practical features include a 150-litre front storage compartment, while the cabin has a 15.6-inch central touchscreen and an 8.8-inch digital instrument display. Higher grades offer additional parking and driving assistance functions for the Chinese market.

The TX also supports vehicle-to-load output of up to 6.6kW, allowing its battery to supply external electrical equipment.

Its emergence comes ahead of Jetour’s expected late-November Australian brand launch, with the T1 and T2 already holding local vehicle approvals ahead of anticipated showroom arrivals in early 2027. Approval does not confirm every listed powertrain will be offered at launch.

Jetour has also flagged a naming change: a November 18 announcement says the T2 is expected to carry the Jetour 20 badge in Australia. Its local plug-in hybrid specification and inclusion in the initial range remain unannounced. Jetourt has also issued photography of the Jetour 20 in disguise in Sydney.

Australian ROVER filings list the T1 with petrol and plug-in hybrid powertrains. The petrol version pairs a 180kW 2.0-litre turbocharged four-cylinder with a seven-speed dual-clutch transmission. The PHEVs combine a 105kW 1.5-litre turbo-petrol engine with a 150kW front electric motor, while the all-wheel drive version adds a 175kW rear motor. The filing lists “maximum possible” drivetrain outputs of 255kW and 430kW respectively, rather than confirmed combined system ratings.

The T2/20 is listed with an all-wheel drive plug-in hybrid powertrain combining a 105kW 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine with three electric motors: 90kW and 75kW units at the front and a 175kW rear motor. The filing lists maximum possible drivetrain power of 445kW, although that should not be treated as a confirmed combined system output. Australian battery capacity and electric driving range remain unannounced.
